questions.question: Q: How much power did Roman women actually have?

points.text: Formally, women could not vote or hold office. However, they managed households, controlled domestic finances, could own and inherit property, and influential women like Livia shaped political events behind the scenes. Their real power often exceeded their legal rights.

questions.question: Q: What was the difference between cum manu and sine manu marriage?

points.text: Cum manu: the wife passed into her husband's legal control. Sine manu: the wife remained under her father's authority, retaining her own property and family connections. Sine manu became more common over time.

questions.question: Q: How were Roman children raised?

points.text: Children received a bulla at birth for protection. Boys attended school or had private tutors; girls were educated at home. Infant mortality was high, and children from poor families went to work young. Upper-class children had Greek tutors and studied rhetoric.

questions.question: Q: Why was the Vestal Virginhood significant for Roman women?

points.text: Vestal Virgins had unique privileges: they could own property, make wills, vote in some contexts and had the right to be buried within the city. Their sacred duty to tend Vesta's flame gave them extraordinary status in a society where women had limited formal power.

questions.question: Q: What do Roman epitaphs reveal about family life?

points.text: Many epitaphs express genuine love and grief — 'you were my sweetest companion', 'I weep for my daughter'. This challenges the view that Roman marriages were purely transactional, suggesting real emotional bonds within families.

markScheme.exemplarAnswer: Roman women exercised significant real power despite their formal legal exclusion from politics, because social influence, economic independence and religious authority provided alternative sources of power. Legally, women could not vote, hold office or serve in the military — the most formal sources of power in Rome. However, in practice, elite women wielded enormous influence through their husbands and sons. Livia, wife of Augustus, was arguably the most powerful woman in Roman history, advising the emperor, managing his household and securing the succession of Tiberius. Cornelia, mother of the Gracchi, shaped two tribunes who changed Roman politics. These women operated through personal networks and family influence rather than formal institutions, but their impact was undeniable. Economically, women could own and inherit property, run businesses and manage large estates — some women were among the wealthiest individuals in Rome. The Vestal Virgins held unique religious power that translated into legal privileges. However, these exceptions should not disguise the reality for most women. Poor women had far fewer opportunities — they worked in shops, markets and homes with little time for political influence. Even elite women's power was dependent on their male relatives — a woman who lost her husband or father could be vulnerable.
